newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - MoneyGram eyes int'l growth.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - MoneyGram eyes int'l growth.

text.p: MoneyGram Payment Systems Inc is looking towards international markets to realize its growth ambitions, said Chairman and Chief Executive James Calvano.

"There is very strong organic growth taking place internationally and we believe that we are beginning to share in that and starting to gain some (market) share," said Calvano in an interview a few days before the company reports its first quarterly earnings since going public.

While declining to elaborate on projections, Chief Financial Officer John Fowler told Reuters that the last nine months or so have seen year-over-year growth, starting from a low base, of about 45-50 percent on non-domestic, non-Mexico business.

Going forward, he said that "while we don't see any reason why the absolute numbers won't continue to grow at the same kind of rate...the percentage, while strong, may not be the same kind of percentage".
Fowler said that overall transactions were growing at a rate of 15 to 20 percent each year for the industry and that Monygram hoped to "at least" keep pace with that growth.

MoneyGram accounted for about 16 percent of all consumer money wire transfer transactions worldwide in 1995, according to the company. Western Union, a unit of First Data Corp, accounted for about 81 percent.
Forty-four percent of total transactions done by MoneyGram in 1995 were between the the U.S. and Mexico, whereas 11 percent involved other international locations.

Cavalo said MoneyGram already has a presence in 85 countries through a network of some 18,600 agents locations, but is now seeking to increase the depth of its coverage through new agent contracts, particularly outside the U.S. - Mexico corridor.
Three large agent contracts were secured in the second half of 1996: Thomas Cook, the United Kingdom Post office, and Consorcio Oriental, which serves the Dominican Republic corridor.

The U.K. post office -- previously a Western Union domain -- may be the biggest coup yet. According to Calvano, this contract - entered into for a five year period - doubles Moneygram's business in the European market.
MoneyGram will continue to position itself competitively vis-a-vis Western Union, Calvano said. The company currently charges 20 to 30 percent less on average than Western Union.

Fowler said the company hopes to offset the impact on profit margins through volume increases. "Our margins today range somewhere between 18 and 20 percent...and we believe that as we obtain more scale we'll be able to push that upward," he said.
MoneyGram also hopes to add value through added services like pre-paid phone cards available through its agents, and recently announced a calling card pact with MCI Communications Corp.

MoneyGram had revenues of $137.1 million in 1995, of which foreign exchange revenues were $42.8 million. In 1996, Fowler said that foreign exchange revenues were just over 20 percent of total revenues, which "were a more normalized percentage of revenues going forward".
The company earned $1.10 per share in 1995: the First Call mean consensus for 1996 is $0.88 per share.

Moneygram was spun out of First Data under a consent decree signed with the Federal Trade Commission at the time of First Data's merger with First Financial Management Corp, the parent of Western Union.

Under a two-year agreement, MoneyGram still depends on First Data for several "back-room" functions like data processing, but Calvano said the company was actively looking for alternative providers and hoped to reach an agreement before the end of the year.
The company completed its intial public offering in December at an offer price of $12 per share.
Its shares were at 13-1/2 in late afternoon trading on Monday.
((---Kamalakshi Mehta, New York Newsdesk 212-859-1610))
